# Decisions

Each decision with the reason, in the order they were made.

## 2026-10-07: Before Phase 1

**D1. Start from the base ALLaM-7B-Instruct-preview, not from the fine-tuned receptionist model.**
The "no Arabic quality loss" check needs the untouched base as "before"; the receptionist habits (one system-prompt
shape, 6 tools, short WhatsApp replies) are too narrow for a general model. The receptionist data is mixed into the
tool-calling stage instead, and the receptionist model stays a comparison row.

**D2. Arabic tool-calling training data is generated by our own rule-driven pipeline (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash as its base
model), not taken from public sets.** The large public Arabic function-calling sets (HeshamHaroon/Arabic_Function_Calling
and the sets built from it: Sellopale/Arabic_Function_Calling, AISA-AR-FunctionCall, AISA-ArabicFC) were generated with
GPT-4o, whose terms do not allow using its output to build competing models. QCRI's Arabic versions of Glaive and xLAM
are described in their paper but not released. Public sets are used only as tests.

**D3. Tests.** ArabFuncBench (native MSA, 1,000 cases, CC BY 4.0) and AISA-ArabicFC dev (545 cases, five dialects
including Gulf) for tool calling; ArabicMMLU (14,575, 0-shot) and Arabic IFEval (404) for Arabic quality; HUMAIN's
LC-Eval (Arabic multiple-choice and claim verification, ≤16K tokens) and an Arabic needle-in-a-haystack test for long
context; the receptionist test v2, run from the earlier project's repo. All are used for evaluation only; the NC
licences of ArabicMMLU and Arabic IFEval allow that, and none of their text is redistributed here.

**D4. Needle haystack from LC-Eval's Arabic contexts; long-context training text from Arabic Wikipedia.** Keeping the
two apart means the long-context stage cannot learn the test's text. LC-Eval's Arabic texts come from Hindawi books,
so Hindawi text is also kept out of training.

**D5. Tool names and JSON keys stay English** (e.g. `get_prayer_times`): they are code identifiers, and every Arabic
tool benchmark uses them. All user-facing text and argument values are Arabic.

**D6. Environment = the previous project's exact stack** (torch 2.12.1+cu130, transformers 5.17.0, peft 0.21.0,
trl 1.14.0, bitsandbytes 0.50.2, Python 3.12), restored from the local package cache, so results are comparable with
the receptionist runs.

**D7. Long prompts are read in 4,096-token slices into a KV cache reserved once at full size.** Reading 16K
tokens in one pass peaked at 14.6 GB, and the default growing cache fragmented PyTorch's memory pool (26 GB reserved
for 13.5 GB of data). On a 16 GB card shared with desktop apps, Windows then moves memory to the much slower system
RAM: a 16K needle case took 60–220 s instead of 6 s. Slicing gives the same answers (checked: identical replies on 2K,
4K, 8K and 16K needle cases); scores move only by bf16 rounding (up to ~0.5 in log-probability, the same amount as
changing the slice size alone).

**D8. Greedy decoding everywhere** (always the most likely next token), so every run is repeatable. ALLaM sometimes
repeats a line under greedy decoding (seen in Arabic IFEval); this affects every model version equally and is kept.

**D8b. Arabic IFEval replies are generated with llama.cpp from the 8-bit GGUF build (Q8_0), for every model
version.** In transformers with 4-bit weights the 404 replies took ~3 hours per model: greedy decoding sometimes
repeats until the 1,280-token limit, and a batch waits for its slowest reply. llama.cpp gets the exact same token ids
(rendered by ALLaM's tokenizer), decodes greedily one request at a time (repeatable), and Q8_0 is closer to the
original 16-bit weights than 4-bit. Fine-tuned versions get a Q8_0 build with the adapter merged (needed for the
release anyway). The other tests stay on the 4-bit transformers model, the form that is trained.

**D9. LC-Eval multiple-choice options are shuffled with a fixed seed.** The correct option is the first one in 62% of
LC-Eval's Arabic multiple-choice items, so "always A" would score 62%. Shuffling puts the answer in each position about
equally often (chance ~25%) and the order is the same for every model. Claim verification also reports the
"always true" score for reference.

**D10. Tool-calling baseline uses the receptionist project's plain-text tool format** (tools in the system prompt,
`<tool_call>{json}</tool_call>`), the same one behind the base model's 40.0% on the receptionist test. Phase 3 builds a
native template and re-runs the base with it, so before/after compare the same prompt. AISA-ArabicFC's test split has
no answers published, so its dev split (545 cases) is the test here. Our argument normalisation is simpler than the
AISA leaderboard's (no alias tables), so our ArgEM is slightly stricter than theirs.

## 2026-10-07: End of Phase 1

**D11. Long-context training at up to 16K tokens, with the loss computed 1,024 positions at a time and the tensors
kept for the backward pass parked in system RAM ("activation offloading").** Measured (QLoRA rank 16, gradient
checkpointing, batch 1, YaRN ×4): without offloading, 12K is the limit (13.1 GB, 14 s per step) and 16K spills into
system RAM (659 s per step). With offloading, 16K needs 12.1 GB and 21 s per step, and 12K runs as fast as before
(14 s). First measured without offloading; Basel asked whether 16K could fit after all, and it can.

**D12. LC-Eval claim verification is reported but not used as a target:** both versions score at chance (balanced
accuracy 52%) and only change which answer they lean to.

## 2026-10-08: Phase 2 (long context)

**D13. Phase 2 training data is written by ALLaM itself, from Arabic Wikipedia, with no paid API.** (The DeepSeek key
is not funded yet; ALLaM's outputs are Apache-2.0.)
- Long reading: the original ALLaM, shown one short section (no long context), writes two question-answer pairs about
  it; pairs are kept only if the answer's words come from the section, the question ends with a question mark and
  nothing is in Latin letters. The section's article is then placed among other articles to make a 6K-16K-token
  context, with three questions (from three articles) asked as a chat. Each question names its article
  («بحسب مقالة «...»») so it is never ambiguous among other articles. A quarter are multiple choice; wrong options are
  answers to other questions about the same article. The instruction is worded differently from our LC-Eval prompt.
- Replay: the original ALLaM (YaRN off) answers short tasks about other Wikipedia sections; the YaRN model learns to
  give the same answers, to win back the short-text loss YaRN causes (ArabicMMLU −1.4).
- Plain text: ~100 whole long articles, every token trained.
- Kept out: book text (the source of LC-Eval's Arabic part) and invented-fact needles. Articles are split 90/5/5 into
  train/dev/spare by a hash of their id.
Fallback if the generated questions prove too weak: our DeepSeek pipeline, once the key is funded.

**D14. Checkpoint rule for Phase 2, fixed before training:** the checkpoint with the highest long-question score on
the dev set (held-out Wikipedia articles; open questions scored by word-overlap F1, multiple choice by the first option letter
anywhere in the reply) is chosen; on a tie the earlier one. Candidates: every 40th optimizer step and the last one (scoring takes ~15 minutes
per checkpoint; checkpoints are still saved every 20 steps). Replay loss on dev is reported alongside. The tests are
run on the chosen checkpoint only.

Scoring note: the first version read only the reply's first character for multiple choice; the base model writes
«بحسب مقالة ...، ... A. ...», so right answers scored 0. Fixed (first option letter anywhere in the reply) and the
starting point re-scored from its saved replies before any checkpoint was scored.

**D15. Phase 2 result: checkpoint 183 of long_v1 is the long-context model.** Chosen by D14 (dev long score 0.730, the
highest). All four approved targets met: needle 16K 100% (≥ 98%), LC-Eval multiple choice 63.8% (≥ 60%),
ArabicMMLU 68.8% (≥ 67.6%), Arabic IFEval not significantly lower (p = 0.91). Plan B (YaRN only for long requests)
is not needed. Phase 3 continues training this adapter.

## 2026-10-11: Phase 3 (Arabic tool calling)

**D16. Phase 3 design.**
- *Format:* the receptionist model's plain-text format (tools in the system prompt, `<tool_call>{json}</tool_call>`
  lines, results in `<tool_result>` user turns), with the guide in Arabic. The Arabic guide and default system
  sentence were written by our DeepSeek pipeline from the project's English spec (`data/tools/guide.json`); one
  module (`scripts/toolformat.py`) renders the format for training, every benchmark and the Phase 4 server.
- *General tool data:* our DeepSeek V4.1 Flash pipeline wrote a library of 102 tools in 18 everyday domains (tool
  names in English, descriptions in Arabic) and ~3,200 conversations, 4 per call, reasoning off, across seven
  scenarios: one call, parallel calls, chained calls, asking for a missing detail, no tool fits, tool error, and
  follow-up requests; users in Modern Standard Arabic (55%) or Saudi dialect (45%). Rule checks keep a conversation
  only if: tool names and arguments match the schemas (required present, types, enums); no Latin letters in user
  text, and in replies only codes copied from tool results; every number in a reply after a tool call comes from the
  conversation or the results; the scenario holds (e.g. no call in "no tool fits", two calls in one turn for
  "parallel"); and the user turns do not overlap any benchmark request. Tools whose names match a benchmark tool
  were dropped from the library.
- *Mix:* general conversations (5% held out as dev, by generation job) + the receptionist conversations (its own
  train/validation split) + Phase 2 replay (150 long chats, 30 long articles, 400 short answers).
- *Training:* continues the Phase 2 adapter (`runs/long_v1/checkpoint-183`) with YaRN ×4, one pass.
- *Checkpoint rule, fixed before training:* the highest share of right assistant turns on the dev conversations
  (`scripts/tool_dev.py`); on a tie the earlier checkpoint.
- *Budget:* a hard cap of $4.00 for all Phase 3 API use (Basel's key held $4.60); every call's reported cost is
  logged in `data/tools/spend.jsonl`. The pilot cost $0.0002 per conversation.
- *Before/after:* the base model and the Phase 2 model are also run in the new format (`--protocol native`), so the
  comparison uses the same prompt.

**D17. Activation offloading without pinned memory** (12 Oct). Pinned host memory is kept by PyTorch's cache and
grew to 27.7 GB of system RAM during tools_v1, slowing steps from ~6 s to 75–94 s. Unpinned memory: steps back to
5–7 s (and 18–50 s for 16K examples). The run was paused cleanly at step 32 and resumed.

**D18. Phase 3 result: checkpoint 400 of tools_v1 is the release model.** Chosen by D16 (dev 80.9%). Met: ArabFuncBench
and AISA far above base, needle 100%, LC-Eval 64.7%, ArabicMMLU 69.2%, IFEval 42.3%. Missed: receptionist test v2
83.1% against the 85% target (the receptionist-only model: 87.5%; paired p = 0.21). Reported as the cost of a general
model; options for a tuning round are left to Basel.

**D19. Optional receptionist tuning round (tools_v2), rules fixed before training** (12 Oct). Basel runs it when the
PC is free (`scripts/steps_tools_v2.txt`).
- *Data:* a second pass over all 1,095 receptionist conversations, with 500 general tool conversations, 100 long
  question chats, 20 long articles and 200 short replay answers, all drawn word for word from the tools_v1 training
  file (`scripts/toolbuild.py --focus`, 1,915 examples). Dev set unchanged.
- *Training:* continues tools_v1 checkpoint 400, half the learning rate (5e-5), 239 steps, YaRN ×4.
- *Checkpoint rule:* the highest share of right receptionist dev turns among checkpoints whose general-tool dev turns
  are at most 1 point below tools_v1's (86.4%); if none beats tools_v1's 77.1% receptionist turns, tools_v1 stays and
  nothing else is run.
- *Release rule:* tools_v2 replaces tools_v1 only if it reaches 85% on the receptionist test v2 and nothing else
  breaks: ArabFuncBench and AISA right-tool not significantly lower (paired p < 0.05), needle 16K ≥ 98%, LC-Eval
  ≥ 60%, ArabicMMLU ≥ 67.6%, IFEval not significantly lower (`scripts/compare_runs.py`).

**D20. Phase 4 serving design** (12 Oct).
- *One chat template in the model:* `release/chat_template.jinja` (written by `scripts/make_template.py`) turns a
  standard OpenAI request (system, messages with `tool_calls` and tool results, `tools`) into exactly the training
  text. Checked against `render()` + ALLaM's template on 16,224 prompts through transformers (all identical) and on
  12,013 prompts through llama-server (identical except 2, where a past call's argument `250.0` comes back as `250`).
- *llama-server reads the format from the template:* its automatic parser finds the `<tool_call>` markers, returns
  standard `tool_calls`, and from the first `<tool_call>` constrains the JSON to the request's tool schemas (a "lazy
  grammar"). No proxy is needed. Arguments sent as JSON strings (LangChain, the OpenAI SDK) are parsed back, so the
  prompt does not change.
- *A tokenizer flag:* llama.cpp's tokenizer adds a space token after every `<s>` (`add_space_prefix`), which ALLaM's
  own tokenizer does not: through the chat API all 300 sampled prompts had different tokens from training. The release
  GGUFs set `tokenizer.ggml.add_space_prefix = false`; then all 300 matched. (The tests so far sent token ids
  directly, so they were not affected.)
- *16K inside the file:* the release GGUFs carry YaRN ×4 (context 16,384, original 4,096), so no command-line flags
  are needed (`scripts/finalize_gguf.py`, which copies the weights byte for byte with new metadata).
- *Ollama:* version 0.40 serves through llama-server with the GGUF's own template, so `release/Modelfile` has no
  template. `release/Modelfile.go-template` is for older Ollama; Go prints the tool schemas as compact JSON, so it is
  not word for word, and its cost is measured.
- *Served scores:* every benchmark gained a `--server` mode (`scripts/served.py`) that sends the real OpenAI request,
  so the release numbers measure what an app gets: weights, template, tokenizer, parser and grammar together.
